stem: Under IAS 2, at what amount is inventory measured in the statement of financial position?

options.content: The lower of cost and net realisable value
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The higher of cost and net realisable value
options.rationale: This would be imprudent: it could carry inventory above what it can earn.

options.content: Selling price less the expected profit margin
options.rationale: IAS 2 does not use a margin.

options.content: Replacement cost at the year-end date
options.rationale: Replacement cost is not the IAS 2 basis.

explanation: IAS 2 requires inventory to be measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value, so that it is not overstated.

stem: A pump in Tendai's shop cost US\$850. It can be sold for US\$1,100, but selling costs of US\$180 will be incurred. At what amount is the pump included in inventory?

options.rationale: Correct: cost 850 is lower than NRV 920.
NRV is 920 but cost is lower, so cost is used.
Selling price is never used to value inventory above cost.
Selling costs are not deducted from cost.

explanation: NRV = 1,100 − 180 = 920. Cost 850 is the lower figure.
hints: NRV = selling price − selling costs; then take the lower.

stem: Which of the following costs is included in the cost of inventory?

options.content: Carriage outwards paid to deliver goods to customers
options.rationale: Selling and distribution costs are excluded.

options.content: Rent of the warehouse where finished goods are stored
options.rationale: Storage costs are expenses of the period.

options.content: Commission paid to the sales staff
options.rationale: Selling costs are expenses, not part of cost.

options.content: Carriage inwards paid to bring the goods to the shop
options.rationale: Correct: it is a cost of bringing the goods to their present location.

explanation: Cost includes the purchase price and the costs of bringing goods to their location and condition. Selling, storage and administration costs are excluded.

stem: Compared with AVCO, what does FIFO give when purchase prices are rising?

options.content: A lower closing inventory value and a higher profit
options.rationale: A lower inventory would increase cost of sales and reduce profit.

options.content: A higher closing inventory value and a lower profit
options.rationale: Higher closing inventory reduces cost of sales, so profit is higher.

options.content: A higher closing inventory value and a higher profit
options.rationale: Correct: the closing inventory is at the latest, higher, prices.

options.content: The same closing inventory value and the same profit
options.rationale: The formulas give different values when prices change.

explanation: FIFO values closing inventory at the most recent costs; with rising prices cost of sales is lower and profit higher.

stem: Nyasha's shop had 85 units at US\$9 each at the start of the month. It bought 130 units at US\$10 and then 110 units at US\$11. During the month 200 units were sold. Using the **periodic** weighted average cost method, at what amount is the closing inventory valued?

options.rationale: This is the FIFO value of the closing inventory.
This values every closing unit at 10, the price of the middle purchase.
Correct: average cost 3,275 ÷ 325 = 10.0769 per unit × 125 units.
This values the closing units at the opening unit cost.

explanation: Goods available: 85 × 9 + 130 × 10 + 110 × 11 = 3,275 for 325 units. Average 10.0769; closing 125 units × 10.0769 = 1,259.62.
hints: Weighted average = total cost of goods available ÷ total units available.

stem: A tuck shop started the month with 70 sweets cartons at US\$14 each. It bought 140 cartons at US\$15 and then 50 cartons at US\$17, and sold 160 cartons. Using **FIFO**, what is the cost of the cartons sold?

options.rationale: This is the weighted average cost of sales.
Correct: 70 units at 14 plus 90 units at 15.
This takes the latest purchases first, which is not FIFO.
This is the closing inventory, not the cost of sales.

explanation: FIFO sells the oldest first: 70 × 14 + 90 × 15 = 2,330. The 100 cartons left are 50 at 15 and 50 at 17 = 1,600. Check: 3,930 − 1,600 = 2,330.
hints: Cost of sales = goods available − closing inventory, or the oldest layers sold first.

stem: Inventory was counted on 6 January, six days after the year end. What adjustments convert the count value to the year-end value?

options.content: Add purchases received after the year end and deduct the cost of goods sold after the year end
options.rationale: This rolls the count forward, the wrong direction.

options.content: Deduct purchases received after the year end and add the cost of goods sold after the year end
options.rationale: Correct: roll the count back to 31 December.

options.content: Deduct both the purchases and the sales made after the year end
options.rationale: Sales after the year end reduced inventory, so they must be added back.

options.content: Add both the purchases and the sales made after the year end
options.rationale: Purchases after the year end increased inventory, so they must be deducted.

explanation: Purchases since the year end increased inventory (deduct); sales since then reduced it (add back at cost).
hints: Think about what has happened to inventory since 31 December.

stem: Closing inventory at the end of 2025 was overstated by US\$2,000, and the error was corrected in 2026. What is the effect on the profit for the year?

options.content: 2025 profit is understated by US\$2,000 and 2026 profit is overstated by US\$2,000
options.rationale: Overstated closing inventory lowers cost of sales in 2025, raising profit.

options.content: Both years' profit is overstated by US\$2,000
options.rationale: The opening inventory of 2026 is also overstated, which lowers 2026 profit.

options.content: There is no effect on profit because inventory is an asset
options.rationale: Closing inventory is deducted in cost of sales, so profit is affected.

options.content: 2025 profit is overstated by US\$2,000 and 2026 profit is understated by US\$2,000
options.rationale: Correct: the error reverses in the following year.

explanation: Overstated closing inventory reduces 2025 cost of sales. The same figure is the 2026 opening inventory and increases 2026 cost of sales.
hints: Closing inventory of one year is the opening inventory of the next.

stem: When valuing inventory, a gain on one item may be used to offset a write-down on another, and only the total is compared with total cost.
explanation: False. IAS 2 requires the comparison item by item (or group by group); gains are not offset.
hints: Is the comparison made item by item or in total?

stem: In a perpetual inventory system the cost of each issue can be found at the time the goods are issued.
explanation: True. The stores record is updated after every transaction, so the cost of each issue is known immediately.

stem: Match each term to its meaning.

right.content: Cost of goods available divided by units available
The inventory record is updated after every receipt and issue
Selling price less the costs of completing and selling the item
The oldest purchases are assumed to be sold first

explanation: Each is a core inventory valuation term.

stem: Complete the statements.

payload.template: Net realisable value = selling price − costs of {{blank:a}} and selling. Inventory is valued at the {{blank:b}} of cost and net realisable value.

explanation: NRV allows for costs still to be incurred; inventory takes the lower figure on grounds of prudence.

stem: A wardrobe in Rudo's furniture workshop cost US\$3,000 to make. It needs US\$600 of further work to finish and can then be sold for US\$3,450, less US\$250 of selling costs. At what amount should it be included in inventory?
explanation: NRV = 3,450 − 600 − 250 = 2,600, which is lower than cost 3,000, so the wardrobe is valued at 2,600.
workedSolution: 1. NRV = 3,450 − 600 − 250 = 2,600, which is lower than cost 3,000, so the wardrobe is valued at 2,600.
hints: NRV = selling price − further costs − selling costs.

stem: Sipho's hardware stores record for a paint product shows: 60 litres in inventory at US\$40; 10 June bought 100 litres at US\$44; 15 June sold 90 litres; 22 June bought 80 litres at US\$48; 28 June sold 120 litres. Using FIFO in a perpetual system, calculate the total cost of the litres sold.
explanation: 15 June: 60 × 40 + 30 × 44 = 3,720. After this 70 litres at 44 remain. 28 June: 70 × 44 + 50 × 48 = 5,480. Total 3,720 + 5,480 = 9,200. Closing inventory is 30 litres at 48 = 1,440.
workedSolution: 1. 15 June: 60 × 40 + 30 × 44 = 3,720. After this 70 litres at 44 remain. 28 June: 70 × 44 + 50 × 48 = 5,480. Total 3,720 + 5,480 = 9,200. Closing inventory is 30 litres at 48 = 1,440.
hints: Issue from the oldest layer first, and update the layers after each issue.

stem: Using the data of the previous question, calculate the value of the closing inventory using the **perpetual weighted average cost** method (recalculate the average after each receipt; use exact averages and round the final answer to the nearest dollar).
explanation: After 10 June: 160 litres, 6,800, average 42.50; issue 90 = 3,825; 70 litres left, 2,975. After 22 June: 150 litres, 6,815, average 45.4333; issue 120 = 5,452; 30 litres left = 1,363. FIFO would give 1,440; a periodic average would give 1,330.
workedSolution: 1. After 10 June: 160 litres, 6,800, average 42.50; issue 90 = 3,825; 70 litres left, 2,975. After 22 June: 150 litres, 6,815, average 45.4333; issue 120 = 5,452; 30 litres left = 1,363. FIFO would give 1,440; a periodic average would give 1,330.
hints: After the first receipt the average is 6,800 ÷ 160.
The units left after an issue keep that average until the next receipt.

stem: Thandeka's year end is 31 December 2025. Inventory was counted on 7 January 2026 and valued at cost at US\$18,900. Between 1 and 7 January goods costing US\$2,400 were received, and goods were sold for US\$6,000. The shop's gross profit margin is 20% of selling price. Calculate the inventory at 31 December 2025.
explanation: Cost of goods sold = 6,000 × 80% = 4,800. Inventory at 31 December = 18,900 − 2,400 + 4,800 = 21,300. Treating 20% as a mark-up on cost gives 21,500.
workedSolution: 1. Cost of goods sold = 6,000 × 80% = 4,800. Inventory at 31 December = 18,900 − 2,400 + 4,800 = 21,300. Treating 20% as a mark-up on cost gives 21,500.
hints: Margin is a percentage of selling price, so cost = 80% of the selling price.

stem: Name the international accounting standard that sets the rules for the valuation of inventory. (Give the standard number.)
explanation: IAS 2 Inventories requires measurement at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

stem: Explain why inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value rather than at selling price.

points.description: Prudence: profit should not be recognised before the goods are sold
Selling price would include an unearned profit, overstating inventory and profit
Where NRV is below cost a loss is recognised immediately in the period it is identified

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Using selling price would recognise profit before a sale is made, which breaks prudence. Inventory is carried at cost unless its NRV is lower, in which case the expected loss is recognised at once.

explanation: Link prudence to both parts of the rule.

stem: Explain **two** effects on the financial statements of using FIFO rather than AVCO when purchase prices are rising.

points.description: Closing inventory is valued at more recent (higher) prices
So the carrying amount of inventory in the statement of financial position is higher
Cost of sales is lower because older, cheaper costs are charged
So profit for the year is higher (and tax or dividends based on it may be higher)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Under FIFO the closing inventory is valued at the latest, higher prices, so current assets are higher. Cost of sales uses the older, cheaper costs, so profit for the year is higher than under AVCO.

explanation: Closing inventory and profit are both higher under FIFO in a period of rising prices.
hints: Which costs are left in closing inventory under FIFO?

stem: Tatenda says: "We should use FIFO because it reports a higher profit when prices rise." Evaluate his reasoning.

points.description: FIFO does give a higher profit when prices rise
But the higher profit is partly an inventory holding gain, not extra cash, and tax or drawings may increase
AVCO smooths price changes and is simpler for identical goods
The method must be applied consistently and chosen to give a fair view, not to increase profit

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: He is correct that FIFO shows a higher profit when prices rise, but the extra profit arises from the older, cheaper costs and does not mean more cash. It may lead to more tax or drawings. The choice should reflect how goods are used and be applied consistently, not be made to raise reported profit.

explanation: A balanced evaluation accepts the fact but questions the motive.
hints: Does a higher profit mean more cash?

stem:
Tatenda sells car batteries from a shop in Bulawayo. During the year the inventory records show:

| Date | Movement | Units | Unit cost US\$ |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 January | Opening inventory | 220 | 8.00 |
| 15 March | Purchase | 320 | 8.50 |
| 20 June | Purchase | 380 | 9.20 |
| 10 October | Purchase | 120 | 10.00 |
| Year | Sold at US\$14 each | 880 |  |

Tatenda uses a periodic system. Ignore all expenses other than the cost of goods sold.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of batteries in closing inventory.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the value of closing inventory using FIFO.
parts.explanation: The 160 batteries left are the latest: 120 × 10.00 + 40 × 9.20 = 1,568.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The 160 batteries left are the latest: 120 × 10.00 + 40 × 9.20 = 1,568.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the value of closing inventory using weighted average cost (answer to the nearest cent).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Tatenda wants to choose one method for future years. Advise him, using the figures above.

points.description: Identifies that FIFO gives the higher gross profit (4,712 against 4,555.69)
Explains why: prices have risen so FIFO charges older, cheaper costs to cost of sales
Notes that the higher profit does not mean more cash and may increase tax or drawings
Notes that AVCO smooths price changes and is simple for identical items
Gives a justified recommendation and states that the method must be applied consistently

answerSpec.modelAnswer: FIFO gives the higher gross profit (4,712 against 4,555.69) because prices rose during the year, so the older, cheaper batteries are charged to cost of sales. The extra 156.31 is not extra cash and may increase tax or drawings. AVCO smooths the price changes. Tatenda should choose the method that best reflects the way the batteries are sold (oldest first) and use it consistently.

parts.explanation: A balanced recommendation uses a figure and mentions consistency.

explanation: This item compares FIFO and AVCO in a periodic system and asks for a justified recommendation.
hints: Cost of goods available = opening inventory + all purchases.
Cost of sales = goods available − closing inventory.
